title: Tenali Raman and the Theft of Wells (Español)

keywords: tenali raman and the theft of wells
full_text:
During a scorching summer in the empire of Vijayanagara, the capital suffered a sudden and inexplicable water shortage. While the Tungabhadra River ran low, several communal wells in the poorer artisan quarters ran completely dry overnight, leaving potters, weavers, and common laborers in distress.

Disturbed by the crisis, King Krishnadevaraya summoned his chief municipal warden, an arrogant officer named Rudrappa.
Rudrappa bowed low and offered a bizarre explanation:
'Your Majesty, the heat of the season is so intense that several public wells have cracked and mysteriously dissolved into subterranean chasms! It will require thirty thousand gold coins from the imperial treasury to construct new wells immediately!'

The King, anxious for his subjects, was about to sign the gold disbursement when Tenali Raman stepped forward with a solemn expression:
'Maharaj, the chief warden's report is profoundly alarming. Indeed, I have noticed that not only have the wells vanished, but thieves have been active under the cover of night. Just yesterday, three full stone wells were seen being carried down the western highway on the backs of thirty pack-bullocks!'

The court erupted in murmurs. King Krishnadevaraya frowned:
'Tenali, art thou mad? How can any thief steal a stone well and carry it on a bullock?'

Tenali bowed with humble gravity:
'Your Majesty, if a stone well can dissolve into thin air as the warden claims, it surely can also be dug up, loaded onto bullocks, and sold to private agricultural estates outside the city walls!'

Tenali then led the King, the ministers, and the royal guards on an unannounced inspection of the private sugarcane plantations belonging to none other than Warden Rudrappa.
There, in the lush, green fields, waterwheels were turning vigorously, pumping thousands of gallons of cool, fresh water from newly dug underground conduits that secretly diverted water from the public city wells! Rudrappa had been selling public water to wealthy orchardists at extortionate prices!

Caught red-handed, Rudrappa fell to his knees in the mud, trembling and confessing his fraud.
King Krishnadevaraya ordered the diversion canals broken immediately, returning abundant water to the artisan quarters. Rudrappa was dismissed and fined double the cost of public repairs.

The King laughed heartily and rewarded Tenali with a gold necklace:
'Only Tenali could use a thief's own impossible tale to catch him in the act!'
moral: Corrupt officials who siphon public resources find their embezzlement exposed when forced to follow their own absurd excuses. [ES]
